after.title: Preprint: Knowledge, Attitudes, and Practices of Advance Care Planning in Patients with Neurosurgical Conditions and Their Caregivers
after.authors: Huynh, V. A.; Lim, M. J. R.; Ong, S. E.; Lim, A.; Koh, G. C. H.; Foong, P. S.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Saw Swee Hock School of Public Health, National University of Singapore, Singapore
after.abstract: Introduction: Advance care planning (ACP) enables quality end-of-life (EOL) care that reflects patients' values and preferences. However, ACP remains limited among individuals with neurosurgical conditions -- such as stroke, glioma, or metastatic brain tumours -- who often experience rapid decline and short prognoses. When ACP discussions occur only after cognitive deterioration or acute events, opportunities for meaningful conversations are lost. This study aims to assess the baseline knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP) of ACP among neurosurgical patients and their caregivers in Singapore. Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional survey of 30 patients with symptomatic intracerebral haemorrhage (SICH) or brain tumours at the National University Hospital and their caregivers. Using validated ACP engagement questionnaires, we assessed participants' KAP, and readiness on 5-point Likert scales (1 lowest - 5 best), alongside nine ACP knowledge statements. Results: Patients demonstrated below-average ACP knowledge (mean = 4.1 / 9) and largely neutral attitudes (3.2 / 5) and perceptions (3.1 / 5). Misconceptions were common, including beliefs that ACP documents are legally binding, that preferred care cannot be delivered without ACP, and that ACP is solely a doctor's responsibility. Consequently, both patients and caregivers showed low levels of ACP engagement. Conclusion: The findings highlight the need to introduce ACP education and conversations earlier in the care journey, especially for individuals at risk of cerebrovascular or cardiovascular events. Early engagement, particularly among those with hypertension or other risk factors, presents a crucial window for preparing patients and families for future care decisions.

after.title: Preprint: Pediatric Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Incidence During and After COVID-19 Social Distancing in Korea: A Nationwide 16-Year Interrupted Time-Series Analysis
after.authors: Choi, I. Y.; Jeon, Y.; Lee, I. K.; Kim, K.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Seoul National University College of Medicine
after.abstract: Background Pediatric out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) is a rare but devastating event. However, the extent to which large-scale public health interventions, such as COVID-19 social distancing policies, affected the incidence of pediatric OHCA remains unclear. Methods We conducted a nationwide interrupted time-series analysis using data from the Korea Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest Registry (2008-2023). The primary outcome was the monthly incidence of OHCA among individuals aged 0-18 years. The study period was divided into three phases: pre-intervention (January 2008-February 2020), social distancing (March 2020-April 2022), and post-lifting (May 2022-December 2023). We used segmented Poisson regression, adjusted for population size and seasonal variation, to estimate changes in monthly incidence at each policy change and reported the results as incidence rate ratios (IRRs). To determine whether these changes differed by age, we compared children with adults (19-64 years) and elderly individuals ([≥]65 years). Results Of the 456,839 registry entries, 10,965 were pediatric OHCAs, of which 6,891 underwent resuscitation in the emergency department. The crude incidence was 7.04, 7.14, and 8.35 per 100,000 person-years in the three phases, respectively. Before the pandemic, incidence rose slightly (annual IRR 1.006 [95% CI 1.001-1.012]; P = 0.032). At the implementation of social distancing, incidence fell immediately (IRR 0.926 [95% CI 0.865-0.991]; P = 0.027), without a significant change in slope (P = 0.081). After restrictions were lifted, incidence rose immediately (IRR 1.138 [95% CI 1.048-1.235]; P = 0.002) and then declined gradually (monthly IRR 0.993 [95% CI 0.988-0.999]; P = 0.023). These changes were confined to children aged 1-11 years (implementation IRR 0.812 [95% CI 0.666-0.991]; post-lifting IRR 1.562 [95% CI 1.278-1.909]). The pattern of change differed significantly by age group (P < 0.001), mainly because incidence rose in children, but not in adults or elderly individuals, after restrictions were lifted. Conclusions Nationwide social distancing was associated with a transient decrease in pediatric OHCA incidence, which was concentrated among children aged 1-11 years and was followed by a rebound above the expected level after restrictions were lifted. Surveillance of pediatric OHCA should account for abrupt changes in children's daily environments, including the closure and reopening of schools and childcare facilities.

after.title: Preprint: Antimicrobial stewardship strategies to optimise antibiotic prescribing in primary care: physicians awareness, beliefs, and strategy use
after.authors: Borek, A. J.; Palacz-Poborczyk, I.; Kuzminska, J.; Luszczynska, A.; Kloda, K.; Babicki, M.
after.abstract: Background: National efforts to promote antimicrobial stewardship (AMS) and prevent antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in primary care need strengthening. Research supports clinician-targeted AMS strategies to optimise antibiotic prescribing, but implementing them in clinical settings is challenging. Aim: Assessment of primary care physicians' awareness of, use of, and beliefs about evidence-based AMS strategies, and perceived barriers and facilitators to implementing them in a country with high antibiotic consumption rates (Poland). Methods: A pre-registered observational survey study. Eligible physicians worked in primary care in Poland for 6+ months and were recruited via professional networks and social media. Data were collected through a pre-piloted online questionnaire and analysed descriptively. Results: 270 physicians (68.2% Specialists/Residents in Family Medicine) participated. Respondents were aware of the threat of AMR (88%), the importance of AMS (93%) and their role in AMS (89%). They most recognised, utilised, perceived as effective, and recommended rapid diagnostic tests, clinical guidelines, and scales/criteria. Respondents reported high familiarity but lower engagement with communication strategies, national actions, education/training, and campaigns. Delayed prescriptions were the least used and recommended. Main barriers were time constraints and insufficient awareness of which strategies to implement. Recommended strategies included tests, guidelines, scales/criteria, AMS action plans for general practices, patient communication resources, and promoting awareness of AMS and its role in high-quality care. Conclusion: Awareness and use of evidence-based AMS strategies among physicians working in Polish primary care clinics appear high. Improvements may require reaching disengaged physicians, increasing uptake of underutilised strategies, and strengthening the impact of already used strategies.

data.summary: added: Preprint: Automatic classification of seizure adequacy in electroconvulsive therapy: A proof-of-concept study

after.title: Preprint: Automatic classification of seizure adequacy in electroconvulsive therapy: A proof-of-concept study
after.authors: Panah, M.; Jessen, B. L.; Rand, A.; Jansen, T.; Jorgensen, M. B.; Morup, M.; Jorgensen, A.
after.abstract: Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is the most effective treatment of a range of severe mental dis-orders and is annually given to more than a million patients worldwide. Dosing of the electrical charge is critical for efficacy and side-effect burden; however, it is currently based on manual assessment of seizure quality and exhibits substantial clinical heterogeneity. Here, we collected 1,000 ECT session electroencephalograms (EEG) from 130 individual ECT patients and made an expert-level classification of the EEGs into actionable seizure quality categories (null-response [0], threshold [T], and adequate [A]). We then trained a range of machine learning algorithms on the raw EEG data to classify the EEGs into these categories and tested for classi-fication accuracy. The highest performing algorithm was able to classify the seizures with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curves of >0.9 for both the 0 vs. T and the T vs. A categories corresponding to excellent discrimination. In contrast, the accuracy of predicting seizure quality in subsequent treatments was only moderate. The addition of clinical variables to the models, such as demographics, anesthesia and anticonvulsant exposure, did not improve model performance. These results provide proof-of-concept of machine learning classification of seizure adequacy in ECT based on raw EEG data. The findings could pave the way for the de-velopment of more objective and personalized decision-support tools in ECT.

after.title: Preprint: Middle Temporal Gyrus Neurite Microstructure and Scam Susceptibility in Older Adults Without Dementia
after.authors: Leguizamon, M.; Zhang, B. Y.; Custer, R. M.; Molinare, C. P.; Oyen, E.; Noriega-Makarskyy, D. T.; Axelrod, J.; Lim, A. C.; Wu, C.; Agarwal, M.; Salminen, L. E.; Choupan, J.; Mosqueda, L.; Han, S. D.
after.abstract: Background: Financial exploitation is a prevalent public health concern among older adults, and emerging evidence links vulnerability to gray matter macrostructure and white matter microstructure, including within brain regions and networks implicated in early Alzheimer's disease. Although diffusion tensor imaging is sensitive to age-related variation in brain microstructure, its scalar metrics cannot distinguish among the tissue properties contributing to observed differences. Neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging (NODDI) models distinct tissue compartments, yielding estimates of neurite density, dendritic complexity, and extracellular free water. Methods: This study examined associations between scam susceptibility and NODDI metrics using ultra-high-field 7-Tesla imaging in 116 older adults without dementia. Neurite density index (NDI), orientation dispersion index (ODI), and free-water fraction were quantified within seven a priori regions of interest linked to early Alzheimer's disease. Multivariate regressions evaluated associations between scam susceptibility and NODDI metrics, adjusting for age, sex, education, and global cognition, with multiple comparison correction within each metric. For significant regions, post-hoc hierarchical regression models tested whether NODDI metrics explained variance beyond regional cortical thickness, total gray matter, and total intracranial volume. Results: Greater scam susceptibility was associated with higher NDI ({beta}=0.30, pFDR=.025) and lower ODI ({beta}=-0.28, pFDR=.044) in the middle temporal gyrus (MTG). No other regions survived correction. Additionally, MTG NDI and ODI explained variance beyond macrostructure measures. Conclusions: These findings identify NODDI metrics as novel microstructural correlates of scam susceptibility beyond macrostructure, supporting investigation of their relevance to financial vulnerability in older age.

after.title: Preprint: Physical and psychosocial outcomes in children with limb loss 2-years after the 2023 Kahramanmaras-Türkiye earthquakes
after.authors: Watson, F.; Sariyildiz, A.; Sayici, E. N.; Metin, O.; Kundakci, B.; Bull, A. M.; Kedgley, A.; Basaran, S.
after.abstract: Introduction: The 2023 Kahramanmaras-Turkiye earthquakes resulted in many paediatric amputations. While prosthetic provision following disasters has been described, little is known about longer-term physical and psychosocial outcomes in children with earthquake-related limb loss. Aim: Evaluate health-related quality of life, prosthesis experience, pain, and function approximately two years post-amputation. Method: Retrospective analysis was conducted of children with earthquake-related limb loss who attend the XXX Center. Socio-demographic and amputation-related data, psychological status, outcome scores for pain, the Paediatric Quality of Life Inventory (PedsQL) and the Trinity Amputation and Prosthesis Experience Scales (TAPES) were included. Results: Fifty-six children (50% female; 13.7{+/-}5.0 years old) were included. Children had unilateral upper limb loss (n=15), unilateral lower limb loss (n=31), bilateral lower limb loss (n=7), or combined upper and lower limb loss (n=3). Data were obtained 2.3{+/-}0.4 years following amputation. Median child-reported PedsQL scores were 72.3/100.0, with high social functioning (85.0/100.0) but lower emotional functioning (60.0/100.0). No differences in PedsQL outcomes were found between limb loss groups. Children rated their physical and emotional quality of life higher than carers rated them. TAPES median scores were 50.0/75.0 for psychosocial adjustment, 16.0/36.0 for activity restriction, and 34.5/45.0 for prosthetic satisfaction. Children with unilateral lower limb loss demonstrated superior adjustment and prosthetic satisfaction than children with unilateral upper limb or bilateral lower limb loss (p<0.05). Conclusions: Children demonstrated favourable physical, social, and school-related quality of life 2.3 years after the earthquakes. However, emotional wellbeing remained affected, highlighting the importance of long-term mental health support alongside prosthetic and rehabilitation services.

after.abstract: White matter hypointensity on T1-weighted MRI (T1-WMHypo), a putative marker of white matter pathophysiological changes, has been less systematically investigated than the widely studied T2-weighted fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (T2-FLAIR) hyperintensity lesions. Here, we built the lifespan normative reference and assessed the clinical significance of T1-WMHypo across various brain disorders using a large multicenter dataset. We first established lifespan normative reference for T1-WMHypo volume by 34,148 healthy individuals (aged 4-85 years). Then, in 7,587 patients across 21 neurological and psychiatric disorders, normative reference-derived deviations revealed disease-specific patterns, with marked deviations in neurological diseases. Deviations of T1-WMHypo volume contributed to differential diagnosis, larger deviations correlated with brain atrophy, cognitive impairment, and poorer outcomes in various brain disorders. Elevated burden of T1-WMHypo volume predicted poor medication response in Parkinson's disease and accelerated disability progression in multiple sclerosis. These associations persisted after adjusting for conventional T2-FLAIR hyperintensity lesions. T1-WMHypo deviations provide an individualized marker of white matter pathophysiological changes, offering novel insights for precision medicine across development, aging and brain disorders.

after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Neurology, Washington University School of Medicine, St. Louis, MO, USA
after.abstract: Importance: Leg dystonia affects 50-80% of children with cerebral palsy (CP), but severity assessment remains subjective and time-consuming. Objective tools are urgently needed to quantify leg dystonia severity in clinical care and clinical trials. Objective: To develop and validate a deep neural network (DxToniaNet) for leg dystonia severity estimation using 2D clinical video recordings. Design, Setting, and Participants: We retrospectively analyzed video recordings of 298 children with cerebral palsy undergoing a seated hand open-close task as part of routine clinical care (Center 1: 193 videos, 720p/30fps; Center 2: 105 videos, 4K/60fps). Videos were rated for leg dystonia severity by a group of 7 experts using the Global Dystonia Rating Scale (GDRS) leg subscore (range 0-40) which has a minimum clinically important difference (MCID) of 4 points. Videos displaying leg dystonia (median expert GDRS score [≥]1) were used to develop and test a machine learning model (DxToniaNet) for estimating leg dystonia severity. Open-source software (OpenPose) estimated bilateral knee, ankle, and toe coordinates, normalized for height and camera positioning, and 69 variance and amplitude features were calculated based on established expert-cited features of leg dystonia. A neural network, DxToniaNet, was developed, trained and validated using 5-fold cross-validation on Center 1 videos before final testing on independent Center 2 videos. Main Outcome(s) and Measure(s): Mean absolute error (MAE), root mean square error (RMSE), and accuracy in differentiating between videos with clinically meaningful differences in GDRS scores were calculated relative to experts' median GDRS scores. Results: When estimating experts' leg GDRS scores in testing data, the proposed machine learning (ML) model yielded a MAE of 1.71 {+/-} 1.68 and RMSE of 2.21 {+/-} 0.34 (significantly less than the GDRS MCID of 4), and 90-94% accuracy in differentiating between videos with greater than a 4-point difference in the GDRS. Conclusions and Relevance: We have demonstrated that DxToniaNet can accurately estimate leg dystonia severity compared to experts' assessments with a small (clinically insignificant) error margin. Our methodology supports generalizability since DxToniaNet was developed and tested using independent videos datasets from different centers, recorded under different conditions. In the future, DxToniaNet may help facilitate standardized leg dystonia severity estimation in clinical care and clinical trials.

data.summary: added: Preprint: How inherited variation shapes human disease trajectories

after.title: Preprint: How inherited variation shapes human disease trajectories
after.authors: Urbut, S. M.; Truong, B.; Khurshid, S.; Hornsby, W.; Rehm, H. L.; Ellinor, P.; Natarajan, P.; Parmigiani, G.; Gusev, A.
after.abstract: Although inherited variation is fixed at birth, its effects on health change with age and differ between common and rare variants. Here, we introduce Mendelnoulli, a longitudinal model that combines the age-dependent effects of polygenic and monogenic variation on health records, separating how much disease each individual accumulates overall from diseases to which they are prone. Mendelnoulli further allows polygenic and monogenic components to exert different influences on latent disease trajectories. We apply the model to 348 diseases, 36 polygenic scores, and 34 monogenic conditions across three biobanks and provide an atlas of the age-dependent effects of inherited variation on common human diseases. We show that polygenic effects change significantly with age, with Mendelnoulli improving held-out one-year discrimination for all 28 diseases tested compared with a model whose polygenic effects are constant over age (median AUC 0.95 vs 0.92). For individuals with no prior diagnoses, Mendelnoulli identified 8.6 more of every 100 new cases than that model, when each flagged the 5\% at highest risk. For genes with an established disease, Mendelnoulli selected that disease for 27 of 30 genes and ranked it first for 17 (7 expected by chance), and recovered known differences in timing, such as earlier breast cancer effects for BRCA1 than BRCA2 (peak 48 vs 66 years). Mendelnoulli provides a unified model of common and rare genetic influences on disease trajectories across the life course.

after.title: Preprint: "Wow, this could be massive": Donor-Conceived Families Experience with Unexpected Recontact for Risk of Inherited Cardiac Conditions
after.authors: Mitchell, L. A.; Ruscigno, A.; Mulhern, S.; Yeates, L.; Macciocca, I.
after.abstract: Introduction: Recontacting families post-gamete donation, after a genetic diagnosis is made in the donor, can create complex challenges for healthcare providers and families. However, there is little literature that explores the family experience. This study aimed to explore the experiences of parents and donor-conceived young people navigating the recontact process and undergoing predictive genetic testing for an inherited cardiac condition. Methods: Semi-structured interviews were conducted to explore participants' experiences in unexpectedly being recontacted and undergoing predictive genetic testing for an inherited cardiac condition. Interviews were recorded and transcribed verbatim. A reflexive thematic analysis was performed. Results: Thirteen participants agreed to be interviewed, nine were parents and four were donor conceived young people. Four overarching themes were identified: (1) Out of the Blue, (2) A ripple effect on the family, (3) Calm after the storm, (4) Beneath the Ripples: the psychological impact. Discussion: Interviews provided insights into fertility services recontact and the predictive genetic testing process. From the themes, we conceptualize a ripple effect model. Findings highlight how cardiac genetics and fertility services are evolving, and the critical role of genetic counselors. The recontact process affects the entire family. However, most participants adapted and moved forward from this event.

after.title: Preprint: Ontology-Based SEA-CDM Integration for Vaccine Clinical Trials: Query, Similarity, and Design Recommendation
after.authors: Zhu, J.; Yeh, F.-Y.; Zheng, J.; He, Y.
after.abstract: ClinicalTrials.gov provides valuable information for vaccine research, but fragmented data structures and inconsistent vaccine naming complicate systematic cross-trial analysis. The Study-ExperimentAssay Common Data Model (SEA-CDM) provides a standardized structure for biomedical study data, while biomedical ontologies supply semantic relationships among concepts. We extracted 9,147 vaccinerelated study records from the Aggregate Analysis of ClinicalTrials.gov (AACT) database, mapped their records into SEA-CDM, and linked vaccine products and reported adverse events (AEs) to the Vaccine Ontology (VO) and Ontology of Adverse Events (OAE), respectively. Building on the existing Ontology-based SEA Network (OSEAN), we organized the integrated data into relational tables and a Neo4j knowledge graph while retaining links to original registrations. We evaluated three applications to assess semantic trial retrieval, context-aware AE ranking and trial similarity, and trial design recommendation. First, VO-based query expansion retrieved 41 candidate RNA vaccine trials compared with 16 using exact VO identifier matching. Second, a context-aware AE ranking model incorporating SEA-CDM features and VO-derived vaccine families improved recall@10 from 0.317 to 0.383 over a frequency-based baseline. TransE and CompGCN embeddings achieved Hits@10 of 0.950 and 0.946, respectively, for retrieving trials sharing the same VO identifier within disease-specific candidate sets. Third, an ontology-based clinical trial design recommendation model was developed using several machine learning methods under leave-one-Material-out evaluation across 23 vaccine classes, although performance varied across classes. These findings demonstrate how structural and semantic integration can support multiple clinical trial analyses using vaccine studies as a case study. This framework provides a foundation for extending ontology-supported data integration and analysis to other clinical research domains.

after.title: Preprint: Reliability-Aware Clinical Relation Learning for Uncertainty-Robust Multi-Label Chest X-ray Classification
after.authors: Jin, Y.; Liu, T.; stephen, m.
after.abstract: Background: Automated multi-label classification of chest radiographs is complicated by overlapping imaging findings, noisy report-derived labels, and changes in disease co-occurrence across clinical settings. Existing clinical-hierarchy methods can encode label relationships, but a rigid hierarchy may conflate categorical membership with empirical association and propagate annotation errors. Methods: We investigated Reliability-Aware Clinical Relation Learning (ReCaRL), a graph-assisted framework for multi-label chest radiograph classification. An image encoder produces initial finding scores, while a graph constructed from training-label associations provides reliability-weighted, confidence-gated updates. Uncertain annotations are handled with observation masks. The evaluation compares flat, weighted, graph-based, and hierarchy-penalty baselines, with internal and external discrimination and calibration assessments. Results: In the internal evaluation, ReCaRL achieved macro AUROC 0.821 and macro AUPRC 0.437, compared with 0.812 and 0.423 for the masked/weighted baseline. Mean AUROC across five common findings was 0.865 versus 0.858. External testing yielded AUROC 0.799 and AUPRC 0.409. Post-hoc calibration reduced the internal Brier score from 0.113 to 0.102 and the external expected calibration error from 0.082 to 0.061, without changing AUROC or AUPRC. Conclusions: Reliability-aware graph propagation and confidence gating were associated with modest improvements in multi-label chest radiograph classification relative to the matched masked/weighted baseline. Post-hoc calibration improved probability reliability in the reported evaluations. The findings do not establish a benefit in prospective clinical decision-making.

after.title: Preprint: Enrollees and Early Lessons from an Agentic Healthcare Platform with Physicians in the Loop
after.authors: Shen, Z.; Ramachandran, A.; Hsiang, E.; Gill, J.; Miller, R.; Stark, N. R.
after.abstract: Agentic healthcare platforms that combine large language models with physician oversight are growing quickly, but little is known about who uses them. We characterized 3,223 enrollees of Lotus AI, a free, physician-supervised agentic platform, who completed onboarding, messaged the agent, and had a linked health record between February and July 2026, and compared them with national benchmarks. Median age was 51 years and 62% were male. Chronic condition prevalence exceeded 2024 National Health Interview Survey estimates in every age band by 4 to 7 percentage points; 18% had a functional or symptom-defined disorder; among the 30% with four or more ambulatory visits in the prior year, care was spread across nearly five providers, with 44% meeting a threshold for high fragmentation. Users with functional disorders generated 1.8 times as many physician escalations and 2.6 times as many laboratory orders as other users, but no more prescriptions. This profile differs from the younger, predominantly female populations reported for direct-to-consumer telemedicine. It moves chronic disease management, functional disorder pathways, and care coordination from aspirations to design requirements, and we argue that deployed AI care platforms should characterize their populations against national benchmarks early.

after.title: Preprint: BenchmarkHub: an open-source platform for reproducible evaluation of large language models in healthcare
after.authors: Alvarez-Arenas, J. I.; Jimenez-Carretero, D.; Sanchez-Cabo, F.
after.abstract: Background: Large language models (LLMs) are solely judged by their scores on biomedical benchmarks, yet these scores are rarely reproducible since the prompts, inference settings and model builds are seldom reported. We developed BenchmarkHub, an open-source platform for auditable evaluation of language and vision-language models for biomedical research. Methods: BenchmarkHub is a Python web application (Django 5.2, SQLite) released under the MIT licence and available at https://github.com/juanjuanignacio/benchmarkhub. The application can be accessed through a browser interface, a set of command-line tools and a REST API, so interactive exploration and scripted pipelines produce identical, comparable records. The platform samples questions with fixed seeds, runs models directly or as tool-using agents in a code sandbox, grades answers with deterministic rules and stores every prompt, reply and tool call. The interface provides a leaderboard to rank performance of the models, allowing model comparison without any preexisting programming knowledge. Findings: We used BenchmarkHub to evaluate 12 open-weight models in five experiments on 15 biomedical benchmarks (11 text, two multimodal and two computational biology) and two general benchmarks. The pooled accuracy ranged from 46.1% (95% CI 43.0-49.3) to 80.9% (78.3-83.3). Re-grading the responses with simple answer-extraction rules lowered a model's accuracy by up to 33.1 percentage points, leading to a reorder of the leaderboard. Published scores were found for 23 out of the 143 benchmark/model combinations tested. The accuracy measured by BenchmarkHub was lower than in the published results in 19 out of the 23 available comparisons. The effect of four prompting protocols (1: default prompt; 2: asking the model to answer the letter only; 3: chain-of-thought prompting; 4: three-shot prompting) changed MedQA accuracy by up to 11.3 points but was not significant after multiple-testing correction with 150 questions. We also tested the impact of ablation on benchmarking using the MMMU benchmark dataset. Removing images lowered the accuracy by 18.0 and 19.3 points respectively for the two strongest models. Finally, the accuracy of agentic benchmarks using a sandboxed interpreter increased on computational biology tasks by 36-63 points. Interpretation: Benchmarking is essential to assess the impact and validity of LLMs for medical applications. BenchmarkHub allows a fair and rigorous comparison of models across established datasets, including the possibility to upload their own datasets. The suite includes visual tools to ease model comparison and ranking without any programming knowledge. Self-hosted infrastructure that records every choice and parameter makes benchmark claims checkable without data leaving the institution.

after.abstract: Background: Emergency tracheal intubation is common and high risk. Although guidelines recommend using a video laryngoscope to intubate critically ill adults, whether a hyperangulated or standard-geometry blade is more likely to achieve successful intubation on the first attempt remains unknown. Research Question: Does the use of a video laryngoscope with a hyperangulated blade increase the incidence of successful intubation on the first attempt among adults undergoing emergency tracheal intubation, compared to use of a video laryngoscope with a standard-geometry blade? after.title: Preprint: Evidence availability for 1-year obesity treatment-initiation decisions: an estimand-aligned Bayesian longitudinal network meta-analysis
after.authors: Yin, X.; Dai, M.; Xia, Z.; Liu, D.; Huang, G.; Li, X.; Wang, X.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Emergency Medicine, Xiangya Hospital, Central South University
after.abstract: Background Obesity pharmacotherapy strategies differ in maintenance dose, titration, and lifestyle support, but existing syntheses primarily compare drugs rather than treatment-initiation decisions. We assessed 1-year weight reduction, permanent discontinuation, and incremental dose-related trade-offs while mapping the availability of eligible trial evidence. Methods We searched eight databases and two trial registries through October 2026 for randomised trials (at least 12 weeks) of obesity pharmacotherapy initiation in adults with overweight or obesity. Maintenance, withdrawal, and switching trials were excluded. Two reviewers independently selected studies, extracted data, and assessed bias and certainty. Bayesian longitudinal network meta-analysis estimated treatment-policy-compatible weight change at 52 weeks. Additional analyses examined discontinuation, dose escalation, titration, lifestyle support, and diabetes-related attenuation. The study was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261532130). Findings We included 180 reports from 178 trials (196 randomisation units; 81,014 participants). Only 78 units reached the 1-year evidence layer, 50 informed the primary longitudinal model in adults without diabetes, and 45 of 160 target strategies had non-extrapolated 52-week estimates. Placebo-adjusted weight reductions were greatest with retatrutide 12 mg (-19.80 percentage points, 95% CrI -21.81 to -17.78), tirzepatide 15 mg (-16.87, -18.07 to -15.51), and cagrilintide-semaglutide 2.4/2.4 mg (-16.37, -18.10 to -14.70). Only tirzepatide 15 mg and semaglutide 2.4 mg had high-certainty evidence. Thirteen of 32 strategies increased adverse-event-related permanent discontinuation versus placebo; none increased all-cause discontinuation. Five of 22 adjacent dose steps had at least 0.80 probability of adding more than 2 percentage points of weight reduction. Eight 1-year titration contrasts and three trials of randomised lifestyle-support increments were identified. Weight reduction in adults with type 2 diabetes was 62% of that without diabetes (ratio 0.62, 95% CI 0.58-0.66). Interpretation Evidence directly supporting 1-year obesity treatment-initiation decisions remains limited. Higher-dose and multi-receptor strategies achieve substantial weight reduction, but certainty and discontinuation trade-offs vary. Better treatment-policy reporting and randomised evidence on titration and lifestyle support are needed.

after.authors: Wamalwa, P. N.; Menbere, K.; Oeba, M. B.; Saumu, W. M.; Laigong, P.; Omar, A.
after.abstract: Background: Thyroid dysfunction is a common endocrine comorbidity in type 1 diabetes (T1D), yet most evidence on its burden and biochemical patterns comes from higher-income settings. Data among African children and young adults with T1D remain limited. Objective: To determine the prevalence and pattern of thyroid dysfunction and examine demographic and diabetes-related factors associated with thyroid dysfunction among children and young adults with T1D in Kenya. Methods: We conducted a multicentre cross-sectional study among children and young adults with T1D aged [≤]34 years attending four diabetes clinics in Kenya. Serum thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) and free thyroxine (FT4) were measured. Thyroid status was classified as euthyroidism (normal TSH and FT4), subclinical hypothyroidism (elevated TSH with normal FT4), overt hypothyroidism (elevated TSH with low FT4), subclinical hyperthyroidism (low TSH with normal FT4), overt hyperthyroidism (low TSH with elevated FT4), or discordant TSH-FT4 profiles that did not meet these predefined biochemical categories. Prevalence estimates with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated, and multivariable logistic regression examined associations with age, sex and duration of diabetes. Results: Among 244 participants with paired TSH and FT4 measurements, 77.5% (n=189) were euthyroid. Twenty-seven participants (11.1%; 95% CI 7.7-15.6%) had biochemically defined thyroid dysfunction: 18 (7.4%) had subclinical hypothyroidism, 5 (2.0%) overt hypothyroidism, and 4 (1.6%) subclinical hyperthyroidism. No overt hyperthyroidism was identified. An additional 28 participants (11.5%) had discordant TSH-FT4 profiles. Hypothyroidism accounted for 85.2% of biochemically defined thyroid dysfunction and was predominantly subclinical (78.3%). Age, sex and duration of diabetes were not significantly associated with thyroid dysfunction in adjusted analyses. Conclusion: Thyroid dysfunction affected approximately one in nine Kenyan children and young adults with T1D and was predominantly hypothyroid, particularly subclinical hypothyroidism. Discordant TSH-FT4 profiles were also frequent, underscoring the importance of careful biochemical classification and confirmation of abnormal thyroid-function tests.

after.title: Preprint: Prevalence of Self-Reported Auditory Dysfunction Among Call Center Employees and Its Association with Shift Work Across Various Call Centers in Cairo, Egypt, March 2026
after.authors: HAKIMHUSSIEN, M. H.; abdel kareem, a.; halim, a.
after.abstract: Abstract Background The rapid, unregulated expansion of the call center industry in developing countries has increased occupational health risks for young adults, particularly with regard to auditory health. Prolonged exposure to acoustic trauma, long working hours, and the high intensity nature of call center work can negatively affect young adults at the start of their working lives and may contribute to permanent noise induced hearing loss (NIHL). This damage is often irreversible but preventable if identified at an early stage. This study aims to evaluate the burden of auditory impairment among call center employees in Egypt and to propose evidence based mitigation strategies. Methods A pilot cross sectional study was conducted among employees of various medical call centers over approximately three months (January to March 2026). Participants were recruited through voluntary (self selected) sampling. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire on work history, and statistical analysis was performed to examine associations with work duration and intensity. Three semi structured, open ended interviews were conducted in March 2026 to explore the symptoms in greater depth. Results Forty six call center employees completed the questionnaire. The most frequently reported symptoms were mishearing words (82.6%), difficulty understanding speech in background noise (80.4%), needing others to repeat themselves (78.3%), and sensitivity to loud sounds (78.3%); 60.9% reported tinnitus. Higher auditory symptom severity was associated with a history of acoustic shock (Mann Whitney U = 344.0, p = .004) and with greater cognitive symptom burden (Spearman's {rho} = .416, p = .004), but not significantly with shift type (p = .177), years of work (p = .885), or daily and weekly working hours. Qualitative interviews described auditory strain that builds through the shift, disrupted sleep, informal coping, and the absence of employer guidance or symptom reporting pathways. Conclusion and Recommendations Self reported auditory symptoms were common in this preliminary sample of call center employees and were associated with acoustic shock exposure and cognitive symptom burden, but not significantly with shift pattern or length of service. Because the study was cross sectional, relied on self reports, and used a small volunteer sample (pilot study), the findings cannot establish causation or true prevalence. Recommended measures include acoustic shock limiters with incident reporting, audiometric screening that prioritizes at risk employees, safe volume education with regular breaks, and educational programs on auditory hazards and early warning signs to prevent actual auditory damage. Larger multi site studies with audiometric confirmation are also needed. Keywords: noise induced hearing loss; call center employees; occupational health; auditory dysfunction; tinnitus; acoustic shock; shift work; Egypt

after.title: Preprint: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus and Risk of Colorectal Cancer: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
after.authors: Wang, S.; Porter, A.; Ge, L.
after.abstract: Epidemiologic studies suggest that type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is associated with an increased risk of colorectal cancer (CRC). However, prior meta-analyses have relied heavily on studies published more than a decade ago and have often combined distinct epidemiologic effect measures. We conducted an updated systematic review and meta-analysis of observational studies published from January 2012 through January 2026 evaluating the association between T2DM and incident CRC. PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, CENTRAL, and Scopus were searched, and eligible studies reporting associations between T2DM and CRC were included. Effect estimates were synthesized separately using random-effects models to calculate pooled estimates with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Sex-specific and leave-one-out sensitivity analyses were also conducted. Fourteen studies were included, comprising nine cohort and five case-control studies; six reported odds ratios (ORs), seven reported hazard ratios (HRs), and one reported a standardized incidence ratio (SIR). T2DM was associated with higher odds of incident CRC (OR, 1.28; 95% CI, 1.13-1.46) and a higher hazard of incident CRC (HR, 1.27; 95% CI, 1.23-1.31). The study reporting an SIR also showed higher CRC incidence among individuals with T2DM (SIR, 1.40; 95% CI, 1.39-1.45). Sex-specific analyses generally showed positive associations in both females and males, and sensitivity analyses supported the robustness of the pooled findings. Overall, T2DM was associated with an increased risk of incident CRC, with a consistent direction of association across distinct epidemiologic effect measures. These findings provide updated evidence supporting consideration of T2DM as a marker of increased CRC risk and may inform CRC prevention strategies among individuals with T2DM.

after.authors: Denier, N.; Grieder, M.; Jann, K.; Borel, P.; Dendorfer, S.; Florineth, G. A.; Adorjan, K.; Federspiel, A.; Wiest, R.; Soravia, L. M.; Walther, S.; Bracht, T.

after.abstract: Objective: To examine whether longitudinal changes in frontoparietal (FP) - subgenual anterior cingulate cortex (sgACC) joint temporal complexity differ between sgACC hemispheres in patients undergoing accelerated TMS (aTMS) and untreated healthy controls. Methods: Twenty-four patients with current depressive episodes and fifteen healthy controls underwent 7T resting-state fMRI at baseline and follow-up. Patients received aTMS localized to the left DLPFC using Beam-F3. The same bilateral FP time series was paired separately with left and right sgACC time series. Bivariate multiscale sample entropy (bMSE) across scale factors a1-a10 was summarized by trapezoidal integration as a complexity index (bMSE-CI). The primary test was the Group x Time x sgACC Hemisphere interaction in a mixed repeated-measures ANOVA. Scale-specific interactions and clinical Spearman correlations were evaluated with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction. Change scores were follow-up minus baseline. Results: The bMSE-CI Group x Time x Hemisphere interaction was significant (F(1,37) = 6.043, p = 0.0188, partial Eta squared = 0.140). Mean left/right bMSE-CI changes were -0.286/+0.124 in patients and +0.323/+0.112 in controls. Of ten scale-specific three-way interactions, only a2 survived FDR correction (q = 0.0435). No baseline or change-score bMSE-MADRS association survived the specified FDR corrections. A random-intercept-only mixed-model sensitivity analysis did not reach statistical significance for the three-way interaction (p = 0.0718). Conclusion: FP-sgACC joint temporal complexity showed hemisphere-dependent longitudinal differences between patients undergoing aTMS and healthy controls. These exploratory findings motivate further evaluation of bMSE as a candidate measure of longitudinal neural change in depression. Independent replication, more precise reliability estimates, and prospective validation of clinical relevance are needed.

after.authors: Evans, W. D.; Ulasevich, A.; Mohammed Gimba, I. S.; Francis, S.; Szabo, J.; O'Sullivan, S.; Bernard, D.
after.abstract: Cervical cancer is the leading cause of cancer death in women in 26 countries, including in sub-Saharan African countries. Cervical and other cancer risks can be greatly reduced through timely HPV vaccination and early screening. But it continues to pose a significant public health challenge in LMICs such as Nigeria. This study reports on the implementation and evaluation of a pair of social media behavior change campaigns to increase HPV vaccination amongst girls ages 9-14 and reduce vaccine hesitancy amongst girls and their parents in Bauchi state, Nigeria. The primary objectives are to conduct a quasi-experimental evaluation of the social media campaign; to examine the effect of higher versus lower levels of campaign exposure on HPV vaccination and related outcomes; to determine whether the social media campaign followed its planned theory of change; and to identify which social media messages were most effective in promoting HPV vaccination. We implemented an HPV vaccination social media promotion campaign, using videos designed to encourage parents to vaccinate their daughters, at scale in Bauchi state on the Meta and TikTok social media platforms. We used a quasi-experimental design, a heavy-up approach, that experimentally manipulated the level of social media content delivered in Bauchi. We used the Virtual Lab platform, an open-source platform that uses social media to recruit participants using advertising and creates panels of respondents for data collection through an online survey, and also collected social media metrics including impressions and engagement. The campaign was effective in increasing HPV vaccination rates from 69% at baseline to 86% at endline over 2 campaign phases that spanned approximately 3 months. Based on GEE modeling, we found that higher levels of engagement with the campaign were associated with higher vaccination rates at midline and endline. Pro-vaccine attitudes and reduced vaccine hesitancy also predicted higher vaccination rates. Also, the campaign produced additional HPV vaccinations at low cost: Adjusted for campaign exposure cost of $0.81 per additional vax in campaign phase 1, $2.10 per vax in phase 2, and $2.40 for the total campaign period. Evidence from this study indicates that social media may be an effective strategy to promote HPV vaccination at low cost. Future rigorous trials using experimental methods are needed to further evaluate social media to promote HPV vaccination.

The primary objectives are to conduct a quasi-experimental evaluation of the social media campaign; to examine the effect of higher versus lower levels of campaign exposure on HPV vaccination and related outcomes; to determine whether the social media campaign followed its planned theory of change; and to identify which social media messages were most effective in promoting HPV vaccination. We implemented an HPV vaccination social media promotion campaign, using videos designed to encourage parents to vaccinate their daughters, at scale in Bauchi state on the Meta and TikTok social media platforms. We used a quasi-experimental design, a heavy-up approach, that experimentally manipulated the level of social media content delivered in Bauchi. We used the Virtual Lab platform, an open-source platform that uses social media to recruit participants using advertising and creates panels of respondents for data collection through an online survey, and also collected social media metrics including impressions and engagement. The campaign was effective in increasing HPV vaccination rates from 69% at baseline to 86% at endline over 2 campaign phases that spanned approximately 3 months. Based on GEE modeling, we found that higher levels of engagement with the campaign were associated with higher vaccination rates at midline and endline. Pro-vaccine attitudes and reduced vaccine hesitancy also predicted higher vaccination rates. Also, the campaign produced additional HPV vaccinations at low cost: Adjusted for campaign exposure cost of $0.81 per additional vax in campaign phase 1, $2.10 per vax in phase 2, and $2.40 for the total campaign period. Evidence from this study indicates that social media may be an effective strategy to promote HPV vaccination at low cost. Future rigorous trials using experimental methods are needed to further evaluate social media to promote HPV vaccination.

after.authors: Mahfuz, S. A.; Al Mahfuz, S.; Roy, S. K.; Rahman, H. I.; Nahar, A.
after.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-based computer-aided detection (CAD) of tuberculosis (TB) on chest X-ray (CXR) may standardize screening and triage in settings with few radiologists but its accuracy in clinical cohorts remains uncertain. We searched five databases (PubMed, ScienceDirect, IEEE Xplore, OpenAlex, Lens.org) on 15 March 2026 for studies published between January 2020 and March 2026, and we appraised these studies using QUADAS-2. Evaluations from clinical cohorts with complete 2 x 2 data and a microbiological or composite reference standard for all participants were pooled using a bivariate random-effects model, with 95% prediction intervals. We accounted for overlapping participants by performing a post hoc analysis with one evaluation per cohort and used GRADE to assess the certainty of the evidence. No protocol was prepared or registered. We included 21 studies (26 evaluations of AI models). Nine evaluations from three independent cohorts were pooled. Pooled sensitivity was 0.896 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.874 to 0.915, prediction interval 0.798 to 0.950) and pooled specificity was 0.689 (95% CI 0.642 to 0.732; prediction interval 0.499 to 0.831). Both confidence intervals include the World Health Organization (WHO) triage thresholds (sensitivity 90%, specificity 70%). When a screening study with partial verification was added, pooled specificity increased to 0.735. Eighteen of 24 assessed evaluations were at high risk of bias and only 1 of 21 studies was prospective, fully verified, externally validated and met the WHO thresholds. Certainty of evidence was low for sensitivity and very low for specificity. A subsequent PubMed search found additional eligible clinical evaluations that were not screened, so the review is incomplete for those studies. In clinical cohorts, AI-CXR sensitivity is close to the WHO triage target, and specificity is close to, but not clearly above, its target. The evidence is pooled across only three cohorts, and specificity varies by product and setting. Thresholds need to be calibrated locally, and prospective, externally validated evaluations are needed before widespread deployment.

after.title: Preprint: Socioeconomic Position, Kidney Outcomes, and Mortality: A Longitudinal Cohort Study from the All of Us Research Program
after.authors: Demiray, A.; Gulmaliyev, I.; Enlice, M. A.; Copur, S.; Berkkan, M.; Mallamaci, F.; Zoccali, C.; Kanbay, M.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Yale University School of Public Health
after.abstract: Background: Socioeconomic position is associated with kidney disease, but it remains unclear whether these differences are greater for worsening kidney function than for a first recorded diagnosis. We examined how household income, education, and neighborhood deprivation relate to mortality and kidney outcomes. Methods and findings: We conducted a retrospective cohort study involving 218,098 individuals using data from the All of Us Research Program, with follow-up to January 1, 2025. Primary outcomes involved all-cause mortality and sustained 40% estimated glomerular filtration rate decline. Secondary outcomes were incident recorded chronic kidney disease (CKD) diagnosis, incident recorded CKD category G3a or worse, and kidney failure. We also evaluated income inequalities and estimated standardized 3-year mortality risks for each baseline kidney state. Median follow-up was 3.62 years for mortality and 2.76 years for kidney outcomes. Among 218,098 individuals, 4,777 deaths, 6,423 sustained declines, 7,870 incident recorded chronic kidney disease diagnoses, 4,716 incident category G3a-or-worse events, and 1,799 kidney failure events were observed. Adjusted hazard ratios (95% CIs) for household income below $25,000 compared with $200,000 or more were 2.68 (2.31-3.12), 3.57 (3.08-4.13), 2.13 (1.90-2.38), 2.15 (1.86-2.49), and 3.08 (2.30-4.11), respectively. Relative index of inequality estimates were approximately twice as large for sustained decline and kidney failure than for recorded CKD diagnosis. Within baseline kidney states, standardized 3-year absolute mortality differences by income did not differ significantly across states. The main limitations are the observational design, baseline creatinine measured up to a year after the survey, and outcome ascertainment from health records that may differ by income. Conclusions: Lower income was associated with higher mortality and greater risk of all kidney outcomes. Education and neighborhood deprivation showed different patterns of association, which supports considering individual and neighborhood circumstances together.

after.title: Preprint: Age and body-mass index account for part of the sex differences in cerebral venous thrombosis
after.authors: Ielapi-Giuffrida, T.; Ruepp, M.; Herzog, L.; Branscheidt, M.; Katan, M.; Thurner, P.; Kulcsar, Z.; Luft, A. R.; Weller, M.; Wegener, S.; Schmick, A.
after.abstract: Background. Women with cerebral venous thrombosis are younger than men and more often present with headache, but the cohorts reporting these differences did not account for age or body-mass index, both of which differ by sex. Methods. Single-center cohort of 219 consecutive adults with confirmed cerebral venous thrombosis admitted in Zurich in 2001-2021. Presentation, imaging and laboratory findings were compared between women and men, and every difference was re-estimated at equal age and body-mass index. Secondary analyses compared functional outcome, residual symptoms and return to work by sex, with an audit of incomplete follow-up. Results. Women (132, 60.3%) were younger (47.3 versus 54.9 years) and had a lower body-mass index (25.9 versus 27.8 kg/m2) than men. Headache (72.0% versus 57.5%) and cortical vein thrombosis (14.4% versus 5.7%) were more frequent in women, but neither association persisted after adjustment (odds ratios, 1.17 [95% CI, 0.54-2.54] and 2.05 [95% CI, 0.59-7.06]). Higher platelet counts (+56 x 109/L [95% CI, 26-86]) and elevated acute-phase markers without documented infection (59.1% versus 33.3%; odds ratio, 2.91 [95% CI, 1.44-5.87]) persisted after adjustment for age, body-mass index and calendar period. Among assessed patients (38% at 6 months), functional independence (86.3% versus 87.5%), residual headache, return to work and recanalization did not differ by sex. Conclusions. At equal age and body-mass index, the female excess of headache and cortical vein involvement was no longer apparent, whereas a higher platelet count and a non-specific acute-phase response remained. Neither translated into a difference in outcome among assessed patients.

after.title: Preprint: Gene-based map of cardiovascular diseases
after.authors: Ozcelik, T.; Kayaalp, B.; Cil, K.
after.abstract: Background: Rare coding variants contribute to cardiovascular disease, but their effects across disease groups remain incompletely characterized. In particular, the influence of functionally and clinically informed variant classification and sex-specific genetic effects on gene-phenotype associations remains understudied. Methods: We analyzed whole-genome sequencing data from up to 483,311 UK Biobank participants across six genetic ancestry groups and eight cardiovascular phenotype groups. Gene-burden testing integrated state-of-the-art missense classification and predicted pathogenic germline variants. We performed combined-sex and sex-stratified analyses, followed by cross-ancestry meta-analysis. We additionally adjusted for cardiometabolic traits in sensitivity analyses, estimated penetrance among qualifying-variant carriers, and assessed genetic prevalence across eight ancestry groups. Results: We identified 86 exome-wide significant gene-phenotype associations: 40 established and 46 novel. Novel associations included EHMT2 with atrial fibrillation, P2RX1 with arrhythmias, P2RY4 with complete atrioventricular block, and NOSTRIN with atherosclerotic heart disease in females. After cardiometabolic adjustment, 60 associations retained exome-wide significance and 18 additional associations emerged, including CDH11, PARVA, and ADAMDEC1 with atherosclerosis-related phenotypes. Conclusions: These findings identify novel cardiovascular gene-phenotype associations implicating purinergic signaling, endothelial nitric oxide regulation, and vascular wall biology. Variant selection shapes penetrance estimates and the interpretation of inherited susceptibility.

after.title: Preprint: Do Rule-Derived Labels Improve Prediction When Reported Labels Are Limited? A Two-Site Machine Learning Study
after.authors: SADI, T. H.; Ruthbah, C. A.
after.abstract: **Background.** Rule derived (weak) labels can enlarge a training set when reported labels are scarce. Their value depends on label quality, on how the extra records shift the training distribution, and on whether the comparison accounts for reported labels set aside for tuning or calibration. **Methods.** We ran an exploratory label-budget experiment on *Escherichia coli* urine cultures from two de-identified electronic health record datasets: Stanford ARMD and UT Southwestern ARMD-UTSW. The task was to predict reported non-susceptibility to cefepime, cefoxitin and ceftazidime (Stanford) and to cefepime and ceftazidime (UT Southwestern). Reported-label budgets of 10%, 25%, 50% and 100% of development patients were drawn over five patient-disjoint outer splits. Logistic regression and histogram gradient boosting were trained with reported labels only, or with added rule-derived labels using equal weights, a tuning-selected weight, class-proportion adjustment or prior-probability correction. These were compared with an all-budget reported-only baseline that used every budgeted reported label for training. Stanford used the inferred labels released with the dataset and a feature set including resistance history. UT Southwestern used researcher-derived labels from Stanford rule text, which were not validated for that site, and an age-only primary model. Brier-score differences were assessed with paired patient-cluster bootstrap intervals. **Results.** All rule-derived labels were susceptible. Equal-weight augmentation lowered mean predicted risk well below observed prevalence (for example, Stanford cefepime at the 10% budget: 0.35% versus 4.85%) and had a higher Brier score than the all-budget baseline in every drug, model and budget summary. The tuning-selected weight did not consistently improve on the all-budget baseline. Its median Brier difference was positive in 38 of 40 drug, model and budget summaries. Its paired intervals lay above zero in 100 of 296 Stanford analyses and 31 of 198 UT Southwestern analyses, and below zero in 3 and 5. The tuning set often selected a weight of zero (146 of 296 and 153 of 198 analyses). At UT Southwestern, the age-only models showed little discrimination (median AUROC 0.49 to 0.54), so those comparisons mainly reflect calibration. **Conclusions.** Under these designs, rule-derived labels did not consistently improve probability prediction over a reported-only model that used the whole reported-label budget for training. Evaluations of weak supervision should include such a baseline and should report calibration as well as discrimination. **Keywords:** weak supervision; limited-label learning; label budget; probability calibration; class imbalance; antimicrobial resistance

after.abstract: Abstract BackgroundCervical cancer, a malignancy affecting the cervix, is the fourth most common cancer and cause of cancer-related mortality among women worldwide. This burden disproportionately affects low-resource regions, where approximately 90% of cases occur. HIV-positive women are at high risk of persistent Human Papillomavirus (HPV) infection and cervical cancer, but screening for this cancer is not yet integrated into HIV care in Sierra Leone. This study aimed to assess the prevalence and risk factors of high-risk HPV infection among women living with HIV (WLHIV) attending Connaught Hospital in Sierra Leone. Methods We conducted a cross-sectional study of women living with HIV aged 25-65 years attending the HIV clinic at Connaught Teaching Hospital in Freetown between September and December 2024. Endocervical swabs were collected for HPV DNA testing. Data was analyzed using R (v4.4.0). Logistic regression analysis was used to determine the independent risk factors for HPV positivity. Results A total of 191 WLHIV were enrolled. The mean age was 36.8 years; 44.5% were single, and 67% were employed. High-risk HPV DNA was detected in 60 (31.4%) (95% CI 25.3%-38.3%) participants, with 50% (30/60)  having multiple serotypes. The most common genotype was HPV 52, followed by 16 and 51. Only 30% of HPV-positive women had genotypes 16 or 18, targeted by the bivalent vaccine. On multivariable analysis, former contraceptive use was independently associated with increased HPV positivity (aOR=4.86, 95% CI: 1.65-17.37,   p = 0.0032). Conclusion The high prevalence of high-risk  HPV infection and predominance of non 16/18 genotypes among WLHIV in Sierra Leone underscore the need to integrate HPV screening within HIV services and consider broader HPV vaccine coverage in Sierra Leone. Former contraceptive use is an independent predictor of HPV positivity, emphasizing the need for robust screening strategies in women using contraceptives.

after.abstract: **Background:** Evidence supporting sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitor use in stage 5 chronic kidney disease (CKD) remains limited because major randomized trials have largely excluded this population. We evaluated associations between SGLT2 inhibitor use and cardiovascular and kidney outcomes in patients with stage 5 CKD. **Methods:** We systematically searched PubMed, Scopus, Cochrane CENTRAL, and Google Scholar through April 10, 2026. Studies comparing SGLT2 inhibitors with nonuse or other glucose-lowering therapies were eligible. after.title: Preprint: Cardiovascular and metabolic trajectories in men engaged in a multidimensional preventive care program: a prospective observational study
after.authors: Bedin, L.; Lepoittevin, M.; Roujansky, P.; Benani, A.; Gounane, R.; Salomon, J.; Sorberts, E.; Steg, G. P.; Bodard, S.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Preventive Medicine, Data Science and AI Lab, Zoi
after.abstract: Objectives: To describe within-individual changes in cardiometabolic, functional and neuroendocrine markers between two standardized evaluations in men engaged in a structured preventive care program, and to examine transitions across clinical risk categories. Design: Prospective observational cohort study using routinely collected data; paired within-individual analyses. Setting: Single preventive health center in Paris, France, offering a standardized multidisciplinary assessment with individualized lifestyle, supplementation and, when indicated, pharmacological recommendations. Participants: 279 men aged 18 years or older with a first evaluation (CU1) between October 2022 and November 2025 and a second evaluation (CU2) by May 2026 (32.3% of 865 eligible men); median interval 13.3 months (IQR 12.0 - 15.6). No exclusion criteria were applied. Primary and secondary outcome measures: Within-individual change in continuous markers (Hodges-Lehmann estimate, 95% CI; Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment over 36 tests) and transitions across fixed clinical thresholds (paired odds ratios). Results: Median age was 51.2 years, BMI 24.5 kg/m2 and SCORE2 2.9%. Visceral adipose tissue mass decreased (delta -49 g, 95% CI -80.5 to -18.5; q=0.006), with small decreases in body mass and fat mass. Handgrip strength increased (right +2.35 kg, 1.70 to 3.00; left +1.70 kg, 1.05 to 2.30; q<0.001). HDL cholesterol increased (+3.5 mg/dL, 2.5 to 4.5; q<0.001), with decreases in the triglyceride/HDL and total/HDL ratios. Blood pressure, LDL cholesterol, fasting glucose (after adjustment), insulin, HOMA-IR, SCORE2 and salivary cortisol and DHEA did not change. The proportion of men below the grip strength reference value decreased from 60.1% to 47.6% (paired OR 0.34, 0.19 to 0.61) and with HDL cholesterol superior to 46 mg/dL from 26.7% to 16.5% (OR 0.25, 0.12 to 0.54). Conclusions: In this selected, health-engaged population of men who completed both evaluations, changes in a favorable direction were observed for handgrip strength, HDL cholesterol and visceral adiposity, whereas blood pressure, LDL cholesterol, glycemic markers and SCORE2 were stable. Without a comparison group, these changes cannot be distinguished from regression to the mean, test retest effects or secular trends.

after.authors: Shouman, A. E.; Saad, R.; Abdalla, A. I.; Sherif, M.; Bdour, M.; Rostom, H.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Faculty of Medicine, Ain Shams University, Cairo, Egypt
after.abstract: Background: Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorders (NMOSD) are a group of neuroinflammatory conditions that affect the nervous system. MLR and PLR are simple inflammatory biomarkers and are studied in many autoimmune and demyelinating diseases. In this study, we investigate the available evidence to determine whether MLR and PLR are higher in NMOSD patients than in healthy subjects. Methods: Systematic review and meta-analysis of studies measuring levels of PLR and/or MLR in both NMOSD patients and healthy controls were conducted. Mean difference (MD) and 95% confidence interval (CI) were used to measure the difference in levels of MLR and PLR between patients and healthy subjects. Results: For MLR, the main meta-analysis yielded a pooled MD of 0.125 [-0.114; 0.363]. I2 was 83.8%. Subgroup meta-analysis of age- and sex-matched studies, demonstrated a pooled MD of 0.066 [0.012; 0.12]. For PLR, meta-analysis revealed a pooled MD of 23.99 [6.03; 41.96]. I2 was 82.3%. Subgroup analysis for age- and sex-matched studies for PLR, showed a pooled MD of 14 [-19.68; 47.68]. Conclusion: The main analysis suggests that MLR is not higher in NMOSD patients than in healthy controls. However, subgroup analysis of age- and sex-matched studies and leave-one-out analysis excluding the outlier study showed a statistically significant MLR increase in patients. PLR was found to exhibit a modest increase in NMOSD patients compared with healthy controls. Nonetheless, subgroup analysis of age- and sex-matched studies showed a statistically non-significant increase. Results should be interpreted cautiously. The available evidence is inconsistent and further research is needed.

after.title: Preprint: PSEN1 loss-of-function variants do not cause early-onset Alzheimer's disease
after.authors: Farinas, A.; Pena-Tauber, A.; Hohman, T. J.; Contreras, A. G.; Jensen, T. D.; Le Guen, Y.; Greicius, M. D.
after.abstract: PSEN1 variants are the most common cause of familial early-onset Alzheimer's disease (EOAD), but it is debated whether they act through a loss- or gain-of-function. Following a recent report of a duo with EOAD carrying a predicted loss-of-function (LoF) stop-gain variant (p.K109*) in PSEN1, we sought to determine whether PSEN1 LoF variants, as a class, cause EOAD. We identified 45 carriers of PSEN1 LoF variants predicted to trigger nonsense-mediated decay in the Alzheimer's Disease Sequencing Project, UK Biobank, and BioVU databases. None of these carriers had a recorded case of early-onset dementia, and 17 were older than 65 years at last follow-up with no dementia or AD reported. Re-analysis of the reported AD-associated variant p.K109* revealed a cryptic splice site predicted to produce an in-frame deletion of 5 amino acids (p.K109_L113del). These results suggest that PSEN1 variants must produce an altered PSEN1 protein product to cause EOAD, while true null LoF PSEN1 alleles do not cause EOAD.

after.title: Preprint: The contribution of Neanderthal ancestry to cancer risk
after.authors: Brand, C. M.; Chen, Y.; Capra, J. A.
after.abstract: Modern human genomes harbor DNA inherited from interbreeding with Neanderthals. Genetic variants inherited from Neanderthals associate with variation in many immune and metabolic phenotypes, two systems with direct relevance to cancer. However, the influence of Neanderthal variants on germline cancer risk has not been comprehensively evaluated. Here, we evaluated genome-wide association study (GWAS) hits for 17 cancer types for Neanderthal ancestry. Twelve cancers have multiple Neanderthal alleles significantly associated with variation in risk. Next, we fine-mapped these risk loci and identified 32 associations across seven cancers where Neanderthal variants are likely causal (>= posterior inclusion probability). Fine-mapped loci include Neanderthal alleles that both increase and decrease cancer risk. Nine of the 32 Neanderthal associations, including the high frequency BNC2 Neanderthal variants, have signatures of adaptive introgression, and several suggest evidence of both mediated and antagonistic pleiotropy. Finally, we tested for enrichment of cancer heritability in genomic regions with Neanderthal ancestry. As expected, Neanderthal variants are depleted of heritability for most cancers. However, Neanderthal variants were enriched for heritability in breast cancer GWAS in both East Asian and Europeans, and this enrichment replicated using individual-level UK Biobank data. These results suggest that Neanderthal alleles that influence germline cancer risk were largely selected against. However, introgressed Neanderthal variants implicated in many cancers persist, potentially due to adaptive pleiotropic effects. This evolutionary perspective provides new insights into the complex evolution and etiology of cancer risk among modern human populations.

after.title: Preprint: Dysregulated B Cell Education Drives Autoimmunity and Immunodeficiency in Down Syndrome
after.authors: Ramba, M.; Buta Panov, S.; Randolph, H. E.; Stewart, O.; Abbad, A.; Ku, A.; Brody, R.; Lee, G. H.; Krammer, F.; Bogunovic, D.
after.abstract: Individuals with Down syndrome (DS) present with both increased rates of autoimmunity and immunodeficiency. To understand this paradox, we first examined lymph node (LN) architecture and immune cell composition in infants with and without DS, as well as peripheral blood B cells from unrelated adults with and without DS. Most strikingly, LNs from individuals with DS exhibited a marked paucity of germinal centers compared with typical lymph nodes. Stromal cells within DS LNs expressed significantly lower levels of the adhesion molecules ICAM1 and VCAM1, accompanied by significantly reduced CXCR5 expression within B cell follicles, suggesting impaired B cell migration and follicular organization. Although fibroblastic reticular cells (FRCs) were present at comparable frequencies in DS and control LNs, MARCO lymphatic endothelial cells (MARCO-LECs), another critical stromal cell population supporting LN architecture, were significantly reduced. In addition, follicular dendritic cells (FDCs), which are essential for antigen retention and B cell selection within germinal centers, were also substantially reduced. To determine the consequences of these abnormalities on humoral immunity, we performed paired single-cell RNA sequencing and V(D)J sequencing of peripheral blood B cells from adults with and without DS. DS memory and CD86+ switched memory B cell populations exhibited significantly elevated reactive oxygen species and PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling gene signatures, coupled with reduced levels of somatic hypermutation in the memory population and increase usage of the autoreactivity-associated IGHV4-34 heavy-chain gene. Collectively, these findings suggest that early-life disruption of LN architecture, characterized by reduced expression of adhesion molecules, selective loss of MARCO-LECs, and depletion of FDCs, impairs germinal center function and B cell education. This defective microenvironment likely contributes to inadequate affinity maturation, as reflected by diminished somatic hypermutation and a more autoreactive B cell repertoire in adults with Down syndrome.

after.authors: Mutter, S.; Dahlström, E.; Luo, X.; Kouki, J. M.; Ju, W.; Nair, V.; Valo, E.; Syreeni, A.; Abdelrahman, Z.; Hill, C.; Smyth, L. J.; Jackson, H. R.; Parton, A.; Harjutsalo, V.; Susztak, K.; Maxwell, A. P.; McKnight, A. J.; McKay, G. J.; Kretzler, M.; Groop, P.-H.; Sandholm, N.; FinnDiane Study Group,
after.abstract: Diabetic kidney disease is the leading cause of kidney failure worldwide, yet the molecular events underlying disease initiation and progression remain unclear. We measured 5,420 circulating proteins in 830 adults with type 1 diabetes and examined their longitudinal associations with onset and progression of kidney disease over 10 years of follow-up. We identified 130 proteins associated with at least one outcome independent of established clinical risk factors, of which 59 replicated in an independent cohort. HAVCR1/KIM-1, GFRA1, CD14 and GDF15 predicted albuminuria onset up to a decade before detectable disease. Albuminuria progression pointed to the kidney-liver axis (ASGR1, RBP4), whereas rapid kidney function decline and incident kidney failure pointed to immune and tumor necrosis factor receptor signaling. Mendelian randomization prioritized UMOD, SORT1, CLSPN, MAST4 and EGF as potential targets. These findings reveal molecular perturbations preceding clinical manifestations of diabetic kidney disease and identify distinct pathways associated with disease progression.

after.authors: Sarwal, R.; Chavan, K. D.; Sharma, J. C.; Manocha, R.
after.abstract:
BackgroundNon-communicable diseases driven by unhealthy lifestyles are a growing and largely avoidable burden among industrial workers. Patient-level evidence on the effectiveness of structured lifestyle programmes delivered alongside standard care -- such as a traffic-light dietary guideline, a Yoga protocol and a daily four-spice culinary infusion -- remains limited. The Integrative Health Clinic (IHC) at ESIC Medical College & Hospital, Faridabad, India, is a family-medicine-style outpatient clinic that follows the 21-item Health Building Lifestyle Guideline and delivers care through a 7-step COM-B-based protocol. We therefore estimated patient-reported relief and compliance with three lifestyle practices in patients attending the IHC.

MethodsWe conducted a retrospective single-arm cohort of patients first seen between February 2025 and 30 September 2026, with follow-up through 4 November 2026. All patients received the three-component lifestyle intervention (advice on spice infusion, diet and Yoga) and were offered follow-up; the 1,466 patients with a usable telephone contact were called for feedback and reinforcement of practices. A physical visit with a coded diagnosis was treated as a valid record. Each patient called was coded once for relief and for spice, diet and Yoga compliance using the most recent definitive answer (YES/NO); calls without a definitive answer ("no response", "not interested") were skipped, and patients with no definitive answer on any call were classified as such. Disease burden, including the screening-detected diagnoses, was counted as patient-condition pairs and classed into 14 systems.

ResultsThere were 4,047 valid visit records from 1,737 unique patients (904 female [52.0%]; mean age 40.3 {+/-} 14.6 years; 833 male [48.0%]; mean age 44.8 {+/-} 15.1 years). Of these, there were 1,035 single-visit [59.6%] and 702 revisit patients [40.4%], i.e. 2.33 visits per patient. The 1,466 analysed patients (763 female [52.1%] and 703 male [47.9%]) comprised 666 revisit and 800 single-visit patients. Their most frequent patient-condition pairs were hypertension (511), obesity (397) and arthritis (268); objective-evidence screening contributed 246 pairs in 233 patients (obesity 161, hypertension 39, anaemia 44, diabetes 2). Of the 1,466 (84.4% of 1,737) patients with a usable telephone contact who were called, 1,016 had a definitive relief answer: 850 (83.7%; 95% CI 81.3-85.8) reported relief and 166 reported no relief. The remaining 450 had no definitive answer. Among the 1,016 patients with a definitive answer, relief was 87.2% (395/453) in revisit versus 80.8% (455/563) in single-visit patients. Treating all 450 patients without a definitive relief answer as no relief, the conservative lower bound of patients reporting relief was 58.0% overall (850/1,466), 59.3% in revisit (395/666) and 56.9% in single-visit patients (455/800). Among the 1,016 patients with practice data, compliance with the spice infusion, diet and Yoga was 77.1%, 83.3% and 81.2%, respectively; counting all 450 non-responders as non-compliant gave conservative estimates of 53.4%, 57.7% and 56.3% for the three practices (n = 1,466). In the responding cohort, relief rose with the five-level compliance dose, from 5.2% (6/115) at dose 0 to 98.2% (326/332) at dose 4 (all three practices plus a repeat visit).

ConclusionsIn this exploratory single-arm cohort, patient-reported relief was more frequent at higher levels of a composite measure that combined the three practices and repeat visits. Because there was no comparison group and all lifestyle components were delivered jointly alongside continuing pharmacotherapy, causality cannot be inferred. The Integrative Health Clinic (IHC) at ESIC Medical College & Hospital, Faridabad, India, is a family-medicine-style outpatient clinic that follows the 21-item Health Building Lifestyle Guideline and delivers care through a 7-step COM-B-based protocol. We therefore estimated patient-reported relief and compliance with three lifestyle practices in patients attending the IHC.

All patients received the three-component lifestyle intervention (advice on spice infusion, diet and Yoga) and were offered follow-up; the 1,466 patients with a usable telephone contact were called for feedback and reinforcement of practices. A physical visit with a coded diagnosis was treated as a valid record. Each patient called was coded once for relief and for spice, diet and Yoga compliance using the most recent definitive answer (YES/NO); calls without a definitive answer ("no response", "not interested") were skipped, and patients with no definitive answer on any call were classified as such. Disease burden, including the screening-detected diagnoses, was counted as patient-condition pairs and classed into 14 systems.

after.abstract:
BackgroundTB eradication strategies in high burden countries need affordable, scalable, and accessible screening tools. This study investigated the diagnostic accuracy of C-reactive protein (CRP), serum amyloid A (SAA), and interferon gamma-induced protein 10 (IP-10) as potential screening tools.

MethodThis cross-sectional diagnostic study investigated stored archived serum samples from three groups of subjects; bacteriology confirmed symptomatic TB group (n=57), probable TB (n=56) and healthy controls (n=60). CRP and SAA concentrations were measured using near point-of-care fluorescence immunoassay (NPOCT-FIA), while IP-10 was measured using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Diagnostic performance of individual and combined biomarkers was evaluated

ResultsReceiver operating characteristic analysis demonstrated excellent diagnostic performance of serum amyloid A (SAA) and C-reactive protein (CRP) for identifying confirmed tuberculosis (TB). Compared with probable TB and healthy controls, SAA achieved an AUC of 0.961 (cut-off >31.0 mg/L), with 96.5% sensitivity and 88.6% specificity, while CRP achieved an AUC of 0.953 (cut-off 21.3 mg/L), with 96.5% sensitivity and 86.0% specificity. Interferon gamma-induced protein 10 (IP-10) showed poor discrimination (AUC 0.545). Combined CRP and SAA achieved 100.0% sensitivity and 83.3% specificity.

ConclusionSAA and CRP met WHO target product profile criteria for TB triage screening.
